summary.text: A linear Diophantine equation sets a sum of unknowns, each with a coefficient, equal to a constant, and only whole-number answers count.
With two unknowns, ax + by = c has a solution exactly when d∣c, where d = gcd (a, b).
Once one solution is found there are infinitely many, and systems of these equations are basic in integer linear programming.

facts.label: How many solutions
facts.value: Infinitely many once one exists, for two unknowns

facts.label: Solving tool
facts.value: Hermite normal form can solve systems of them

items.prompt: You have only 4-cent and 6-cent stamps and need to make exactly 9 cents of postage. What does the solvability rule say?

options.label: It works, as long as you have enough stamps of each kind
It fails, because the shared factor of 4 and 6 does not divide 9
It works, because 4 and 6 add up to more than 9
It fails, because 9 is larger than both stamp values

items.explain: A solution exists only if d∣c, where d = gcd (a, b). Here d is 2, and 2 does not divide 9.

items.prompt: You find one pair of whole numbers that solves a two-unknown linear Diophantine equation. How many other solutions are there?

options.label: None, the pair is the only one
Exactly one more, with the unknowns swapped
Infinitely many more, all generated from the first pair
A finite number that depends on the constant

items.explain: If one solution exists, all the others are given by a formula using an arbitrary integer, and there are infinitely many.

items.prompt: Which description matches a linear Diophantine equation?

options.label: Unknowns with whole-number coefficients are added to equal a constant, and only whole-number answers count
An unknown sits in an exponent, and any real number is an acceptable answer
Unknowns are multiplied by each other and the answer may be a fraction
A single unknown is set equal to a constant, with no whole-number requirement

items.explain: A linear Diophantine equation equates the sum of unknowns with coefficients to a constant, and only integer solutions are of interest.

items.prompt: A delivery planner wants the best whole-number split of trucks across routes under several limits. Why do integer-programming textbooks cover systems of linear Diophantine equations?

options.label: Integer programming only ever deals with one equation at a time
They let the planner ignore the limits and still get an answer
They guarantee the best answer is always a fraction of a truck
Integer programming seeks best whole-number answers to linear systems

items.explain: Integer linear programming finds integer solutions of linear systems that also include inequalities, so systems of linear Diophantine equations are basic in that setting.

items.prompt: A programmer must solve a system of linear Diophantine equations and wants the reduction that is cheaper to compute. According to Richard Zippel, which should she pick?

options.label: Hermite normal form, which only needs a triangular shape
Smith normal form, which reduces to a diagonal shape
Both cost the same, so either one will do
Neither, because no normal form helps with these systems

items.explain: Zippel wrote that only a triangular form is needed, which is the Hermite normal form, and that it is substantially easier to compute than the Smith normal form.

items.prompt: Boxes hold 6 or 9 items and you want a total of exactly 12. Does a whole-number combination exist?

options.label: No, because 12 is not a multiple of 9
No, because 6 and 9 are different sizes
Yes, but only if you use the same number of each box
Yes, because the largest shared factor of 6 and 9 divides 12

items.explain: Here d is 3, and 3 divides 12, so the rule says a solution exists (two boxes of 6).
